units.title: The Big Picture
units.promise: Understand the exchange before learning the documents.

workbook.title: My reasons, my evidence, the employer’s needs
workbook.task: Complete a two-party hiring map, separate private motivations from public role-fit reasons, and create an initial evidence bank.

units.title: Finding and Understanding a Job
units.promise: Read opportunities before investing effort in them.

workbook.title: Opportunity investigation
workbook.task: Inspect two job ads and one suspicious outreach, mark requirements, find official sources, build a fit matrix, and draft one optional cold message.
workbook.output: Annotated posting, safe target shortlist, and personalized cold outreach.

units.title: The Résumé / CV
units.promise: Make relevant experience easy for another person to understand.

workbook.title: Résumé / CV studio
workbook.task: Use a plain sample template, turn evidence into concise bullets, build your own draft in any document editor, and check relevance and truthfulness.
workbook.output: Complete learner-authored résumé or CV; no fake auto-export promise.

units.title: The Cover Letter
units.promise: Explain the connection that a résumé alone may not show.

workbook.title: Cover letter studio
workbook.task: Decide whether a letter is appropriate, annotate a complete model, draft a role-specific letter, then revise it from the hiring manager’s view.
workbook.output: One complete original cover letter and marked revisions.

units.title: How Hiring Works
units.promise: Understand the process and handle the messages around it.

workbook.title: The professional inbox
workbook.task: Move through a realistic inbox: invitation → screening → reschedule → assessment → thank-you → wait → rejection or offer → acceptance/decline.
workbook.output: Message portfolio and correct no-response decisions.

units.title: The Interview
units.promise: Answer questions with real evidence, and understand the conversation.

workbook.title: General and behavioral interview practice
workbook.task: Listen to, transcribe or read a screening/general question; build evidence stories; answer novel behavioral and situational questions; respond to follow-ups.
workbook.output: Three flexible original responses and one revised rehearsal.

units.title: Technical and Role-Specific Interviews
units.promise: Transfer a common communication framework into unfamiliar work.

workbook.title: Role-specific explanation
workbook.task: Choose support, operations, or software/research support; handle a role-specific task and communicate how you reason even when uncertain.
workbook.output: One recorded or typed task explanation and uncertainty check.

units.title: The Final Application
units.promise: Combine the skills in one continuous, believable hiring journey.

workbook.title: One complete fictional application
workbook.task: Pick one Northstar role and proceed through the real connected artifacts, interview branches, recruiter messages and offer/rejection outcomes.
workbook.output: Application portfolio, communication log and next-action plan.

lessons.title: What is a job?
lessons.question: What exactly are people exchanging when they take a job?
beats: Distinguish work, job, occupation, career, role, and position in everyday English.
Show that people supply time, skills, judgment or service; an employer provides compensation and agreed conditions.
Explain employer, employee, manager, recruiter, customer and team in a simple scene.
Mention part-time, full-time, temporary, internship and self-employment as different arrangements, not interchangeable legal categories.
lessons.examplePlan: A scene of a busy shop and a worker, with the same principle applied to a research lab.
lessons.action: Sort five real-world statements into job, career, task, or self-employment; label who contributes what in a shop scene.
lessons.artifact: A completed work-exchange diagram and one original sentence.
lessons.outcome: Explain what a job is without reducing it to either money or passion.

lessons.title: Why do people work?
lessons.question: Is there one correct reason to want a job?
beats: Explore needs (income, safety, autonomy), wants (learning, interest, belonging, growth) and contributions (what one can offer).
Legitimize financial necessity without requiring invented passion.
Explain that motivations can change with circumstances, life stages and job type.
Separate a private reason for needing employment from a role-specific reason for applying.
lessons.examplePlan: Three illustrated applicants with different, equally legitimate priorities.
lessons.action: Choose the three reasons that actually matter to you, separate what you would say privately from what you would say to an employer, and rewrite one reason truthfully.
lessons.artifact: A private needs/wants/contributions reflection plus an authentic job-interest sentence.
lessons.outcome: State a genuine motivation without copying a sentimental interview script.

lessons.title: Why do employers hire?
lessons.question: Why would a business or organization pay someone to work?
beats: Start with work that needs to be done: serving customers, scheduling, producing software, teaching, researching.
Show constraints: money, deadlines, reliability, skills, teamwork, regulations and training capacity.
Distinguish “needs a credential” from “needs a capability”; in some roles credentials are legally required.
Show why a role description lists duties and qualifications.
lessons.examplePlan: Before-and-after scene: work demand exceeds existing team capacity.
lessons.action: Examine an overwhelmed service desk. Pick the actual operational problem, the skills needed, and what proof a candidate could provide.
lessons.artifact: A needs-to-evidence chain with no unsupported claims.
lessons.outcome: Explain an employer’s basic hiring problem in one or two sentences.

lessons.title: Two parties, imperfect information
lessons.question: Why can neither side know in advance whether a job will work?
beats: An applicant knows some of their own needs and capabilities; the employer knows some of the work and conditions.
Documents, interviews, work samples and references reduce uncertainty but never eliminate it.
Discuss unequal bargaining power, scarce opportunities and imperfect hiring decisions without making the learner cynical.
The applicant also evaluates pay, conditions, responsibilities, learning and treatment.
lessons.examplePlan: Split-view cards showing applicant and employer questions; connect at the hiring decision.
lessons.action: Sort ten questions between applicant and employer, then add one question you would personally need answered before accepting.
lessons.artifact: A two-party uncertainty map.
lessons.outcome: Describe hiring as a two-way decision under uncertainty.

lessons.title: What counts as evidence?
lessons.question: How does an employer distinguish a claim from a believable example?
beats: Difference between “I am hardworking” and an observable example.
Experience can come from paid work, school, volunteering, caregiving, projects or internships.
Qualifications and potential differ: some roles require proof or authorization before entry.
Honest relevance beats exaggeration; a beginner can be credible without pretending to be experienced.
lessons.examplePlan: Two miniature candidate profiles, one with paid experience and one with project evidence.
lessons.action: Convert three vague claims ("hardworking", "good at teamwork", "quick learner") into specific, real examples, or mark "no evidence yet".
lessons.artifact: An evidence bank that can be reused in applications.
lessons.outcome: Connect one ability to one concrete supporting experience.

lessons.title: See the whole journey
lessons.question: What happens between wanting a job and deciding whether to accept one?
beats: Map job search → advertisement → application → screening → interview/assessment → offer → decision.
Explain that stages vary by country, employer and role, and some steps are skipped or repeated.
Introduce essential English words: vacancy, apply, requirements, shortlist, interview, offer, reject.
Introduce the fictional company and recurring example learner; let learners choose “learn from zero” or “interview soon” without locking content.
lessons.examplePlan: A single interactive hiring journey map, with stages that reveal a real artifact.
lessons.action: Arrange six hiring artifacts and events into a sensible sequence; flag which stages can overlap or disappear.
lessons.artifact: An annotated hiring journey map.
lessons.outcome: Identify the purpose of the main stages and the English needed at each.

lessons.title: What kind of job?
lessons.question: What are you actually searching for?
beats: Distinguish job title, work function, industry, seniority and work arrangement.
Explain on-site, hybrid, remote, contract, shift, full-time, part-time and internship vocabulary.
Clarify how adjacent job titles can hide similar work and how the same title can differ across employers.
Start with desired tasks, constraints and skills rather than company prestige alone.
lessons.examplePlan: Three similar-sounding advertisements with different actual duties.
lessons.action: Choose preferred tasks, work arrangements, commute limits and eligibility; compare three job titles whose actual duties differ.
lessons.artifact: An honest role-and-constraints profile.
lessons.outcome: Describe a job target beyond its title.

lessons.title: Where openings come from
lessons.question: Where do people learn that someone is hiring?
beats: Company career pages, reputable job boards, campus centers, referrals, networking, recruitment agencies and direct applications.
Explain that a referral introduces a candidate; it is not a guaranteed advantage.
Teach search expressions, filters and how to avoid applying indiscriminately.
Use generic tool categories rather than depending on one paid platform or country.
lessons.examplePlan: Side-by-side mock search results from three sources.
lessons.action: Use a sample careers page, job-board result and forwarded message. Trace each to a legitimate employer-controlled vacancy page.
lessons.artifact: Two useful search queries and one verified vacancy path.
lessons.outcome: Find and recognize a credible opportunity.

lessons.title: Cold outreach: when and why
lessons.question: When should you contact someone who has not invited you?
beats: Distinguish informational outreach, referral requests, speculative applications and direct responses to posted roles.
Decide whom to contact, what useful information to ask for and what a reasonable request looks like.
Explain that outreach is optional, context-dependent and should never become mass spam.
lessons.examplePlan: Two authentic-looking professional profiles and three outreach goals.
lessons.action: Choose the most reasonable contact and request in three situations; identify what should be researched before sending.
lessons.artifact: A contact-and-purpose plan.
lessons.outcome: Differentiate an information request from an unsolicited demand for a job.

lessons.title: Write and follow up on a cold message
lessons.question: What makes a stranger willing to read or reply?
beats: Use a truthful context or shared connection, clear purpose, specific low-burden request and concise close.
Contrast email with LinkedIn-style direct messages; choose channel and register appropriate to the recipient.
Demonstrate one respectful follow-up, appropriate wait, and stopping when there is no reply; no guaranteed response.
lessons.examplePlan: An annotated short cold email, an overlong weak message, a polite follow-up and a no-response branch.
lessons.action: Assemble and personalize a 4–6 sentence outreach message to a fictional worker; write one optional follow-up and choose when to stop.
lessons.artifact: A usable original cold message and follow-up.
lessons.outcome: The message is truthful, specific, respectful and easy to ignore.

lessons.title: How to read a job advertisement
lessons.question: What information is actually in the posting?
beats: Point out role title, purpose, responsibilities, required/preferred qualifications, location, hours, compensation, deadline and application method.
Teach “responsible for,” “required,” “preferred,” “report to,” “eligible,” “experience with.”
Separate plain claims about culture from concrete working conditions.
Read the posting as evidence of the employer’s priorities, not as a guarantee of what the job will be like.
lessons.examplePlan: A full fictional job posting with tappable inline annotations.
lessons.action: Inspect a new posting and highlight duties, required vs preferred criteria, compensation, schedule, location and deadlines; mark missing facts.
lessons.artifact: A marked-up advertisement and three clarification questions.
lessons.outcome: Extract the essential information from an unfamiliar posting.

lessons.title: Requirements, preferences and eligibility
lessons.question: Does a candidate need to meet every bullet?
beats: Separate non-negotiable legal/credential/work authorization requirements from employer preferences.
Discuss “years of experience” as a signal that may or may not be flexible.
Never teach candidates to misrepresent authorization, licenses or qualifications.
Explain when asking the recruiter a precise question is better than guessing.
lessons.examplePlan: Three labeled posting lines: legally required license, essential shift availability, preferred tool experience.
lessons.action: Classify requirements as legal/credential, essential job constraint, or negotiable preference; decide whether to apply or clarify.
lessons.artifact: A requirement matrix and a polite clarification message.
lessons.outcome: Recognize real blockers and avoid treating every preference as mandatory.

lessons.title: Research the employer
lessons.question: What should you verify before applying?
beats: Understand what the organization does, whom it serves and what the advertised team does.
Look for credible information about work conditions, responsibilities, compensation and culture.
Check company identity and vacancy legitimacy; do not send money to get hired or disclose unnecessary sensitive details.
Distinguish a real research finding from vague flattery about mission and values.
lessons.examplePlan: A compact mock company page versus a suspicious recruitment message.
lessons.action: Compare a real-looking employer page and two mock messages, including an urgent paid-equipment scam; identify verifiable signals without guessing from grammar alone.
lessons.artifact: A legitimacy checklist and a safe next step.
lessons.outcome: Describe a reason to apply grounded in actual job information.

lessons.title: Match your evidence to their needs
lessons.question: How can you tell whether you are a plausible candidate?
beats: Create a two-column “they need / I can show” map.
Separate strong evidence, partial evidence, missing skills and transferable skills.
Include non-work evidence without inventing outcomes.
Identify one requirement to address in a cover letter or conversation.
lessons.examplePlan: An editable requirements-to-evidence mapping for a fictional candidate.
lessons.action: Drag four posting requirements beside your real examples; where evidence is missing, mark the gap instead of inventing experience.
lessons.artifact: A truthful match table that feeds the résumé and letter.
lessons.outcome: Make a reasoned fit assessment rather than claim perfect fit.

lessons.title: Choose what to apply for
lessons.question: How do you balance application quality, quantity and time?
beats: Prioritize credible roles by eligibility, fit, urgency, conditions and effort.
Track applications and deadlines; avoid generic spam but do not assume a few perfect applications guarantee success.
Use concise ethical outreach and referrals where suitable.
Know when to broaden roles or revise material if responses are limited.
lessons.examplePlan: A simple three-vacancy comparison and application tracker.
lessons.action: Rank three plausible vacancies using fit, pay, deadline, commute, eligibility and preparation effort; plan where to spend your time.
lessons.artifact: A justified shortlist and simple application tracker.
lessons.outcome: Set a realistic plan for two or three relevant opportunities.

lessons.title: What is a résumé or CV?
lessons.question: Why does a recruiter ask for this document?
beats: A concise record of relevant qualifications, experience, education and projects.
Differentiate common U.S. résumé usage from longer academic CVs and regional uses of the word CV.
The goal is to make relevant evidence easy to find, not to tell an entire autobiography.
Explain human screening and hiring software without claiming magic ATS tricks.
lessons.examplePlan: One résumé and one academic CV shown next to a job ad.
lessons.action: Look at two documents labeled résumé and CV. Identify what changes between a short job-focused résumé and an academic CV; pick an appropriate format for a stated country/role.
lessons.artifact: A document-choice explanation, with country-variation warning.
lessons.outcome: Explain the document’s purpose and recognize format differences.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a résumé
lessons.question: What does each section contribute?
beats: Name and appropriate contact details, summary if useful, work experience, education, skills, projects, certifications and relevant extras.
Order sections according to role and career stage; not every section is mandatory.
Explain reverse chronological organization and plain, consistent formatting.
Show what not to include by default, while warning that photo and personal-detail conventions vary across countries.
lessons.examplePlan: Fully annotated, accessible HTML résumé document with tappable headings.
lessons.action: Tap the annotated sections of two complete sample documents and rearrange a disorganized example for easier reading.
lessons.artifact: A section-order plan that fits a chosen role.
lessons.outcome: Understand a complete sample without imitating every formatting choice.

lessons.title: Describe experience truthfully
lessons.question: How do you turn work into useful evidence?
beats: Distinguish duties from specific actions and results.
Teach action verbs and patterns: action + object + context + outcome.
Use numbers only when true and relevant; good evidence need not be quantified.
Avoid unsupported superlatives, invented achievements, and copied AI language.
lessons.examplePlan: Before/after bullet examples with an explanation panel.
lessons.action: Rewrite bland or exaggerated experience bullets using action, task and result, retaining only evidence the fictional applicant has.
lessons.artifact: Three truthful, readable experience bullets.
lessons.outcome: Write one clear, factual résumé bullet.

lessons.title: No experience, career changes and gaps
lessons.question: What belongs on a résumé when paid experience is limited or different?
beats: Use school, volunteering, projects, internships and relevant responsibilities.
Select transferable skills for a new field; do not disguise a transition.
Address employment gaps only when useful or requested and without forced intimate disclosure.
Distinguish a skill you have used from one you are still learning.
lessons.examplePlan: Two fully annotated example résumés: first-time applicant and career changer.
lessons.action: Choose school, volunteer, caregiving or project evidence for an applicant with no paid experience; handle a gap without fabricating a job.
lessons.artifact: One credible entry-level résumé section.
lessons.outcome: Recognize honest ways to present a non-linear background.

lessons.title: Create and format a résumé
lessons.question: How do you actually make the document?
beats: Use common document editors/templates; teach headings, spacing and editable text rather than a specific app subscription.
Explain when to use PDF or another employer-requested format; check legibility and copyable text.
Avoid unnecessary graphics and decorative layouts for roles that prioritize quick scanning.
Give an accessible checklist for file naming, contact accuracy, spelling, links and privacy.
lessons.examplePlan: A printable simple template alongside a mock export/download menu.
lessons.action: Choose a plain template, fill contact/education/experience sections with safe fictional details, check readability and export instructions.
lessons.artifact: A first résumé draft ready for independent editing in a document tool.
lessons.outcome: Know how to create, export and inspect a readable résumé independently.

lessons.title: Compare, tailor and check
lessons.question: How should a résumé change for a specific opening?
beats: Read two complete annotated sample résumés against one advertisement.
Explain why changing emphasis is legitimate but changing facts is not.
Identify irrelevance, missing evidence, hard-to-read sections and inconsistencies.
Use a practical review checklist without claiming a guaranteed “ATS score.”
lessons.examplePlan: Job ad + two résumé examples; optional “show recruiter’s view” lens.
lessons.action: Compare one generic résumé with a version tailored to a specific Northstar posting; find unsupported keyword stuffing and hidden formatting traps.
lessons.artifact: A concise revision checklist and corrected draft.
lessons.outcome: Judge whether an application résumé answers the employer’s key needs.

lessons.title: Create your own résumé or CV
lessons.question: Can you assemble a clear, truthful document without copying the example?
beats: Offer one minimal job résumé template and one academic CV illustration; distinguish country/industry conventions.
Provide a phrase bank for describing tasks, teamwork, tools and measurable results without inventing numbers.
Explain plain tools (word processor, template, PDF export) and a privacy-first workflow with optional local notes.
lessons.examplePlan: Two downloadable blank layouts and a fully annotated before/after sample.
lessons.action: Populate a worksheet from your evidence bank, construct a document in your own editor and apply a role-specific proofreading checklist.
lessons.artifact: A draft résumé or CV built by the learner.
lessons.outcome: A reader can find relevant, accurate evidence quickly.

lessons.title: What is a cover letter?
lessons.question: Why would an employer want an additional letter?
beats: A short, audience-specific explanation of your interest and relevant evidence.
Sometimes required, sometimes optional, sometimes not used; distinguish attachments, email messages and application-form questions.
Show what a letter adds to a résumé: motivation, fit, context or a career transition.
Explain that long, ornate writing is not an advantage.
lessons.examplePlan: Résume-only application versus an application requiring a cover letter.
lessons.action: Decide whether a cover letter is required, optional, or unnecessary in three situations, and state the useful question a letter can answer.
lessons.artifact: A clear reason to write—or not write—a letter.
lessons.outcome: Recognize when and why to write a cover letter.

lessons.title: Read from the hiring manager’s viewpoint
lessons.question: What does the reader need to learn?
beats: What role is the applicant seeking? Why this job? What evidence fits? Why continue the conversation?
Differentiate generic admiration from a researched connection.
Avoid false certainty about what every hiring manager wants.
Show that a letter is not a rewrite of the résumé.
lessons.examplePlan: One hiring manager’s short review with highlighted questions.
lessons.action: Read an opening from a hiring manager’s viewpoint: highlight evidence and relevance, cross out vague compliments.
lessons.artifact: A hiring-manager read-through annotated by purpose.
lessons.outcome: Identify the essential information without relying on a rigid formula.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a useful letter
lessons.question: How does a concise letter work sentence by sentence?
beats: Practical opening: role, relevant motivation, strongest connection.
Evidence paragraph: one or two concrete experiences and why they matter for this job.
Closing: invitation to discuss, thanks and next step; appropriate professional greeting and sign-off.
Show multiple legitimate structures, formal and natural tone, and country/sector variation.
lessons.examplePlan: Fully annotated letter with optional alternate paragraph order and tone comparison.
lessons.action: Assemble paragraphs from real facts in a sensible order: role, fit evidence, connection, and closing; identify information that belongs in the résumé instead.
lessons.artifact: A structured cover-letter outline.
lessons.outcome: Explain the function of each paragraph, not memorize a script.

lessons.title: Weak versus useful writing
lessons.question: What makes a letter specific and believable?
beats: Contrast generic claims (“perfect fit,” “passionate”) with concrete evidence.
Make one experience relevant to an advertised duty.
Use clear sentences over clichés, flattery and overly complex vocabulary.
Teach honest career-change context without oversharing or apology.
lessons.examplePlan: Two complete letters about the same fictional applicant and role, with annotations.
lessons.action: Compare a formulaic letter with one specific to the role and correct four weaknesses without adding invented enthusiasm.
lessons.artifact: An improved letter excerpt and explanation.
lessons.outcome: Revise an unconvincing cover letter without inventing credentials.

lessons.title: Send a complete application
lessons.question: What should happen just before and after sending?
beats: Check instructions, required documents, filenames, links and deadlines.
Show a concise application email and a short application-form response.
If no letter is requested, do not require one; if asked, adapt the message.
Keep one record of what was sent and where, for later interviews.
lessons.examplePlan: Mock application form, upload checklist and confirmation email.
lessons.action: Check a complete fictional application against the instructions, subject line, file names, attachments and deadline; spot a risky personal-data request.
lessons.artifact: A final submission checklist and concise email.
lessons.outcome: Submit a coherent application packet and retain the details.

lessons.title: Write and revise your own cover letter
lessons.question: Can you write an original letter for an actual set of requirements?
beats: When a letter is requested, select a few strongest links between your evidence and the job.
Show a full sample without prescribing a universal paragraph count or emotional enthusiasm.
Practice editing for specificity, brevity, register, grammar and consistency with the résumé.
lessons.examplePlan: A complete Northstar job posting, applicant evidence bank, and two contrasting finished letters.
lessons.action: Draft a letter from a fictional applicant’s real experiences, revise it after a hiring-manager perspective check, then try your own.
lessons.artifact: A complete original draft and revised version.
lessons.outcome: Each substantive claim is relevant and supported.

lessons.title: Why employers use multiple stages
lessons.question: Why do employers not decide from one document or conversation?
beats: Explain application receipt, eligibility checks, interviews, assessments, references and offers.
Acknowledge variation: screening, behavioral and technical interviews are types, not a fixed three-round ladder.
Understand the applicant’s choice to withdraw at any stage.
lessons.examplePlan: Interactive hiring timeline with branching paths for different roles.
lessons.action: Place the stages of three fictional hiring processes in plausible order and identify what each stage helps assess.
lessons.artifact: A process map with possible variations.
lessons.outcome: Learner can explain why stages differ by employer.

lessons.title: Human and software-assisted screening
lessons.question: What happens to an application before a conversation?
beats: Explain humans, applicant tracking systems, filters, eligibility checks and varied automated ranking tools.
Avoid mythical ATS hacks; favour truthful content, readable layout and role relevance.
Explain that screening is imperfect and a rejection is not proof of personal inadequacy.
lessons.examplePlan: Mock application review with a human reviewer and a rule-based eligibility filter.
lessons.action: Mark what a screening rule could check, what a person still needs to judge, and where information is missing.
lessons.artifact: A screening reality-check worksheet.
lessons.outcome: Distinguish software handling of applicants from guaranteed algorithmic ranking.

lessons.title: Recruiter communication basics
lessons.question: What messages might arrive after you apply?
beats: Recognize confirmation, additional information, availability request, interview invitation, hold, rejection and offer.
Read tone and instructions accurately and respond with clear, concise English.
Notice suspicious pressure, unusual financial requests and unverified senders.
lessons.examplePlan: An inbox containing seven realistic fictional hiring messages.
lessons.action: Classify each message; decide reply/no reply, urgency, and what information can be safely shared.
lessons.artifact: An inbox response plan.
lessons.outcome: Learner can read recruiter instructions without guessing.

lessons.title: The initial screening interview
lessons.question: What does an early recruiter call usually check?
beats: Purpose: basic qualifications, experience overview, interest, schedule, compensation expectations and availability where appropriate.
Phone/video etiquette, concise answers, asking for clarification, and questions about next steps.
Screening is sometimes conducted by the hiring manager or skipped entirely.
lessons.examplePlan: A 10-turn fictional recruiter screening call with purposeful annotations.
lessons.action: Respond to six common screening prompts including schedule and role interest; ask one question about the process.
lessons.artifact: A short recorded or typed screening-call rehearsal.
lessons.outcome: Answers are clear, truthful, and relevant.

lessons.title: Scheduling, confirming and rescheduling
lessons.question: How do you handle interview logistics professionally?
beats: Confirm time, time zone, platform, location, interviewer, accessibility needs or accommodations if relevant.
Write a clear confirmation, request an alternative slot, or reschedule without oversharing.
Explain what not to share with unverified contacts.
lessons.examplePlan: Three recruiter invitation emails with timezone and schedule conflicts.
lessons.action: Compose one confirmation, one reschedule request and one clarification about the interview format.
lessons.artifact: Three short professional messages.
lessons.outcome: No ambiguity about when and how the candidate will attend.

lessons.title: Assessments, interviews and waiting between rounds
lessons.question: What if there is a test, an extra interview or a long pause?
beats: Explain work samples, short assessments, panels, references and extended delays.
Clarify preparation instructions, deadlines, and reasonable boundaries around unpaid work.
Track commitments while continuing other applications rather than assuming silence is failure.
lessons.examplePlan: Recruitment timeline with branching assessment and panel routes.
lessons.action: Decide how to respond to an assessment invitation, ask for missing instructions, and plan preparation.
lessons.artifact: An assessment plan and one clarification email.
lessons.outcome: Candidate understands requirements and retains agency.

lessons.title: Thank-you email after an interview
lessons.question: What is the purpose of thanking an interviewer?
beats: Brief appreciation, specific reference to the conversation, and genuine continued interest.
Explain customary expectations vary across settings; a generic copied note is not a magical advantage.
A thank-you can be unnecessary or inappropriate in some workflows; it should never override explicit instructions.
lessons.examplePlan: Two concise thank-you emails: generic versus specific, with annotations.
lessons.action: Use interview notes to write a 4–6 sentence thank-you email without repeating the résumé.
lessons.artifact: A personal, appropriate thank-you note.
lessons.outcome: Message is specific, respectful and truthful.

lessons.title: When you do not hear back
lessons.question: When should you follow up—and when should you stop?
beats: Respect the timeline the employer gave you and any instructions not to contact.
Write one concise status inquiry after an appropriate wait, then avoid repetitive chasing.
Distinguish ordinary delays, formal rejection and ghosting without assuming motives.
lessons.examplePlan: A timeline showing a promised decision date, one delayed decision and no-response branches.
lessons.action: Choose whether to wait, inquire, or move on in three scenarios; write one appropriate follow-up.
lessons.artifact: A status inquiry and stopping rule.
lessons.outcome: Learner can follow up without demanding an immediate answer.

lessons.title: Rejection: understanding and replying
lessons.question: What does a rejection mean, and should you respond?
beats: Compare automated mass rejection, personal rejection after interview and request to stay in touch.
Optional response: acknowledge decision, express appreciation and genuine future interest without insisting on reconsideration.
Requesting feedback may be appropriate, but feedback is not guaranteed and you may simply move on.
lessons.examplePlan: Three fictional rejection emails with different levels of personalization.
lessons.action: Select which rejections warrant no response, a brief appreciative reply or an optional request for feedback; draft one.
lessons.artifact: An appropriate response—or deliberate no-reply decision.
lessons.outcome: Learner keeps doors open without assuming they were second choice.

lessons.title: Understanding and evaluating a job offer
lessons.question: What exactly are you being asked to accept?
beats: Read salary/pay, hours, start date, responsibilities, location, contract type, benefits and conditions.
Explain acceptance deadlines, questions, negotiation, and cultural/legal differences without giving legal advice.
Remember that an offer is a decision point for the applicant, not an obligation.
lessons.examplePlan: Two Northstar offer summaries with different pay, hours and responsibilities.
lessons.action: Compare two offers against your priorities; identify two points to clarify and choose a reasoned response.
lessons.artifact: An offer decision worksheet and questions.
lessons.outcome: Learner recognizes consequential terms and unresolved details.

lessons.title: Accept, decline, withdraw and preserve relationships
lessons.question: How do you finish an opportunity professionally?
beats: Write accept, decline and withdrawal messages with gratitude, clarity and no unnecessary apology.
Handle competing applications without making promises you cannot keep.
A polite exchange is worthwhile even when no future opportunity follows.
lessons.examplePlan: Three message threads: acceptance, declined offer and withdrawal from consideration.
lessons.action: Draft a concise acceptance, a clear decline and a respectful withdrawal; choose the appropriate delivery channel.
lessons.artifact: Three outcome-specific messages.
lessons.outcome: Each message states the decision unambiguously and respects the other party.

lessons.title: What is an interview really testing?
lessons.question: Why would an employer ask questions after reading the documents?
beats: It can explore evidence, reasoning, communication, motivation and work requirements.
Introduce interview families: background, motivation, behavioral, situational, role-specific and logistics.
There is rarely one universally correct answer; some questions test concrete knowledge or qualifications.
Start building a personal “evidence bank” of authentic experiences, not perfect scripts.
lessons.examplePlan: Seven question cards that reveal the likely purpose behind each.
lessons.action: Match interview prompts to what they are testing (basic fit, evidence of behavior, role-specific skills); note that one round can mix all three.
lessons.artifact: An interview-type recognition worksheet.
lessons.outcome: Recognize the purpose of an unfamiliar question.

lessons.title: The first minutes
lessons.question: How do you begin and manage the setting?
beats: Greeting and introductions; small talk as appropriate, and simple turn-taking.
In-person, telephone and video differences: audio checks, delays, professional requests.
Show etiquette without insisting on one culture’s rules or judging personality.
Teach repair phrases such as “Could you repeat that?” or “Could I take a moment?”
lessons.examplePlan: Short audio-first arrival scenario with transcript and pauses.
lessons.action: Listen to three greetings and choose the clearest natural response; practise checking audio/video, arriving, and asking to repeat a question.
lessons.artifact: A short recorded or typed opening exchange.
lessons.outcome: Manage the opening of an interview in understandable English.

lessons.title: Tell me about yourself
lessons.question: How do you introduce your relevant background without retelling your life?
beats: Explain the hidden purpose: short background → relevant evidence → connection to role.
Show an experienced and a first-time candidate answering differently.
Choose what to omit, how to sequence time, and how to adapt to 30–90 seconds.
Practise a paraphrased follow-up (“Walk me through your background”).
lessons.examplePlan: Interviewer audio + two contrasted expandable sample answers.
lessons.action: Build a 45–60 second truthful introduction from present background, past evidence, and relevance; practise three differently worded prompts.
lessons.artifact: One flexible introduction, not a memorized script.
lessons.outcome: Give a relevant introduction with little or no prompt.

lessons.title: Why this job, why this employer?
lessons.question: How can someone answer honestly without faking passion?
beats: Distinguish personal reasons for employment from reasons this role fits.
Use evidence from employer research, work duties and personal strengths.
Offer legitimate examples: financial stability plus transferable skill, interest in product, desire to learn.
Avoid empty compliments and pretending to know the company’s future.
lessons.examplePlan: Three truthful candidate motivations plus a role advertisement.
lessons.action: Separate "why I need work" from "why this role makes sense"; use an employer fact and your evidence to answer without pretending passion.
lessons.artifact: A role-specific motivation response.
lessons.outcome: Give a credible motivation tied to this role.

lessons.title: Qualifications, strengths and difficult background questions
lessons.question: How do you speak about what you can do and where you are still growing?
beats: Discuss strengths through evidence; distinguish skills from unsupported adjectives.
Handle “weakness,” “little experience,” gaps, career change, or why leaving a job without dishonesty.
Avoid hostile claims about former employers or unnecessary private disclosures.
Explain how to say “I have not done that yet, but I have done ___.”
lessons.examplePlan: Four questions with examples from first-time and experienced candidates.
lessons.action: Transform vague strengths and defensiveness about gaps into evidence-based, concise answers; choose a weakness and explain realistic improvement.
lessons.artifact: Two supported responses and one safe boundary for personal questions.
lessons.outcome: Describe capabilities and limitations credibly.

lessons.title: Past experience: actions and outcomes
lessons.question: How do you answer “Tell me about a time when…”?
beats: Explain a simple story structure: context → your action → outcome/learning.
STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) is an optional organizing aid, not a sacred recitation.
Emphasize one’s actual contribution and avoid inflated results.
Practise a variant prompt to prevent memorized answers.
lessons.examplePlan: A short illustrated work incident with movable story segments.
lessons.action: Arrange a real example into situation, task, action and result; then answer an unfamiliar variation without the labels.
lessons.artifact: One usable evidence story and a transfer answer.
lessons.outcome: Tell a clear, concrete story answering a behavioral question.

lessons.title: Teamwork, conflict, mistakes and pressure
lessons.question: What can stories about difficulty reveal?
beats: Types: collaboration, disagreement, difficult customer, error, changing priorities, feedback, deadline.
Explain responsibility, communication, choice, consequences and learning.
Never teach candidates to invent a dramatic conflict or disclose confidential information.
Provide safe student/project examples for learners without jobs.
lessons.examplePlan: Four short alternative incidents and common interviewer probes.
lessons.action: Choose a respectful way to discuss conflict, feedback, mistakes or pressure; avoid blaming teammates or claiming perfect behavior.
lessons.artifact: An honest difficult-situation answer.
lessons.outcome: Answer at least one challenging behavioral question truthfully.

lessons.title: Situational and judgment questions
lessons.question: What if the interviewer asks what you would do in an unfamiliar situation?
beats: Clarify the problem, relevant constraints, people affected and risks.
Outline a reasonable next action and what information you would seek.
Show how safety, ethics, accuracy and priorities change answers.
Contrast reasonable approaches rather than pretending every scenario has one model answer.
lessons.examplePlan: Fictional service incident and office error with branching decision points.
lessons.action: Given a new scenario, explain what you would clarify, prioritize, do and communicate; compare more than one reasonable response.
lessons.artifact: A structured judgment answer to a novel situation.
lessons.outcome: Respond logically to a new “What would you do if…?” question.

lessons.title: Keep the conversation going
lessons.question: How do you handle follow-ups, questions and unknowns?
beats: Listen, pause, check understanding, ask clarification, and answer follow-up questions directly.
Say “I don’t know” appropriately and explain a reasonable next step.
Ask the interviewer about role expectations, support, working conditions and process.
Handle logistics: start date, hours, location, salary expectations and ending the conversation.
lessons.examplePlan: Three-turn conversation simulator with one surprising follow-up.
lessons.action: Respond to interruptions, unclear wording and follow-up questions; ask one substantive question about responsibilities or support.
lessons.artifact: A two-way exchange with clarification and candidate question.
lessons.outcome: Sustain an interview exchange instead of delivering a rehearsed monologue.

lessons.title: Questions to ask the interviewer
lessons.question: What information do you need before you can make a good decision?
beats: Explain questions about actual tasks, supervisor expectations, training, schedule, success measures and hiring timeline.
Differentiate genuine questions from questions whose answers are prominently stated in the posting.
Explain sensitive topics such as compensation and availability as legitimate, with timing and cultural variation.
lessons.examplePlan: A short interview closing, with two candidate questions and interviewer responses.
lessons.action: Choose three questions you would ask a potential employer; adapt one when the interviewer has already answered it.
lessons.artifact: A shortlist of useful questions.
lessons.outcome: Questions help the applicant evaluate the offer without antagonism.

lessons.title: Behavioral interview rehearsal
lessons.question: Can you respond to unfamiliar wording without reciting a model answer?
beats: Build a small bank of truthful evidence stories before the interview.
Practise follow-ups that probe personal contribution, verification, uncertainty and learning.
Use evidence-first feedback rather than personality, accent or confidence scores.
lessons.examplePlan: Three related interview prompts that demand different emphasis from one actual experience.
lessons.action: Answer one behavioral prompt, reveal an unexpected follow-up, identify unsupported claims, and retry with clearer evidence.
lessons.artifact: Two attempts and an explanation of what improved.
lessons.outcome: Response answers the question, gives specific action and stays truthful.

lessons.title: What makes an interview role-specific?
lessons.question: What changes when the employer tests actual job knowledge?
beats: Distinguish claims about experience from demonstrating domain competence.
Technical might mean coding, troubleshooting, research design, a customer scenario, a sample lesson or a safety procedure.
Interview formats differ: problem-solving, task demonstration, case, portfolio review, whiteboard or trial task.
The course teaches English for explaining competence, not the competence itself.
lessons.examplePlan: Three contrasting role-specific assessment invitations.
lessons.action: Sort four activities into domain-specific demonstration, general behavioral evidence, or recruiter screening; explain why technical tests vary.
lessons.artifact: A classification and one preparation implication.
lessons.outcome: Recognize when general interview preparation is insufficient.

lessons.title: Prepare from the requirements
lessons.question: How do you turn a role advertisement into a practice plan?
beats: Extract the actual tools, responsibilities, constraints and relevant knowledge.
Create an evidence bank: project, skill, portfolio item, process or result.
Make an honest gap plan and locate official or field-specific preparation resources.
Identify role-specific vocabulary and the English for explaining it simply.
lessons.examplePlan: Role ad annotated into skills, artifacts and communication tasks.
lessons.action: Extract tools, competencies and deliverables from a sample posting; create a short practice plan without studying unrelated material.
lessons.artifact: A prioritized role-specific prep plan.
lessons.outcome: Know what to study beyond this general English course.

lessons.title: Explain your reasoning aloud
lessons.question: How do you speak when the answer is not immediate?
beats: Restate the problem and constraints; ask clarifying questions.
Explain approach, assumptions and trade-offs in accessible English.
Check work, acknowledge limits and summarize the result.
Keep speech concise; technical jargon is used when relevant and explained when needed.
lessons.examplePlan: Think-aloud transcript with highlighted good moves and unnecessary rambling.
lessons.action: Explain how you would diagnose a simple work problem before knowing the answer: clarify, reason, test and check.
lessons.artifact: A structured spoken or typed reasoning trace.
lessons.outcome: Make reasoning visible without bluffing.

lessons.title: Three roles, one communication method
lessons.question: What stays constant between very different occupations?
beats: Customer support: handle an unhappy customer without promising what is impossible.
Operations assistant: prioritize conflicting requests and communicate delays.
Technical/research role: troubleshoot a failed process or explain an experiment/implementation decision.
Compare the common structure: understand problem → choose action → explain trade-offs → check result.
lessons.examplePlan: Three interchangeable tabs showing equivalent role scenarios.
lessons.action: Attempt one support ticket, one operations scheduling problem and one basic software debugging prompt; compare the shared communication moves.
lessons.artifact: One selected solution and a cross-role reflection.
lessons.outcome: Recognize general communication patterns in distinct work settings.

lessons.title: Evidence, uncertainty and technical follow-up
lessons.question: What happens when the interviewer presses for proof?
beats: Walk through a project or portfolio artifact: goal, your role, method, outcome and limitation.
Respond to “Why did you choose that?” and “What would you change?”
Admit uncertainty and propose a credible way to verify; don’t invent results or proprietary information.
Teach a transferable “scope → approach → evidence → limits” structure without a fixed script.
lessons.examplePlan: Annotated project brief and two progressively harder follow-up questions.
lessons.action: Practise saying what you know, what you would verify and what you cannot yet claim; answer a technical follow-up without bluffing.
lessons.artifact: An honest uncertainty-and-evidence response.
lessons.outcome: Handle a role-specific follow-up truthfully and clearly.

lessons.title: Technical interview rehearsal
lessons.question: Can you show your process when the domain question changes?
beats: Choose one of three role-specific tasks, each with a clear scope and reasonable difficulty.
Practise thinking aloud, clarifying assumptions, checking work and admitting limits.
Separate linguistic quality from correctness of specialist knowledge.
lessons.examplePlan: Three fictional assessments with short evaluator rubrics and no claim of licensing or job-readiness.
lessons.action: Select one task, explain a proposed solution, inspect model reasoning, and retry with new constraints.
lessons.artifact: A role-specific explanation plus honest uncertainty statement.
lessons.outcome: Shows a sensible process and uses understandable language; expert accuracy requires domain review.

lessons.title: Meet Northstar and choose a role
lessons.question: Can you understand a complete opportunity?
beats: Meet fictional Northstar Services: customer service, operations and software/research support functions.
Choose one position; each has realistic duties, required vs preferred qualifications and conditions.
Use a fictional candidate profile or your own private notes, so beginners need not reveal real personal data.
Research the fictional company and choose what you would verify if this were a real role.
lessons.examplePlan: One company website + three coherent vacancy pages.
lessons.action: Review Northstar company context, compare three role advertisements, and choose a role based on constraints and evidence.
lessons.artifact: A chosen role and justified application plan.
lessons.outcome: Make an informed application choice.

lessons.title: Prepare and submit
lessons.question: Can you present the evidence in writing?
beats: Choose/reorder résumé content appropriate for the selected position.
Write a brief motivation/evidence paragraph; prepare a cover letter if the selected vacancy requests one.
Check truthfulness, contact details, format, filenames and the instructions.
Submit a mock application and receive a confirmation.
lessons.examplePlan: Editable training application packet with résumé snippets, cover-letter fields and submission preview.
lessons.action: Produce a fictional résumé, cover letter only if appropriate, and submission message for the selected role; check factual consistency.
lessons.artifact: A coherent application packet.
lessons.outcome: Produce an internally consistent, role-relevant application.

lessons.title: The hiring conversation
lessons.question: Can you handle an interview beyond rehearsed lines?
beats: Receive and confirm a mock invitation; choose phone/video/in-person version if supported.
Answer background, motivation, behavioral, situational and one role-specific question.
Handle at least one paraphrase or follow-up; ask one employer question.
Adapt challenge to language level: controlled response for A1/A2, freer speaking for B1/B2.
lessons.examplePlan: Five-to-seven-turn structured interview with audio, transcripts and typing alternative.
lessons.action: Respond to a recruiter invitation, complete a screening conversation and one behavioral question, then choose a role-specific challenge.
lessons.artifact: An interview transcript, recording or typed response with self-review.
lessons.outcome: Demonstrate a coherent exchange, including recovery when uncertain.

lessons.title: The decision and what comes next
lessons.question: Can you evaluate an outcome and reuse the skill?
beats: See one believable outcome (offer, another stage, or rejection); never claim hiring likelihood from language feedback.
If an offer appears, review key terms, ask for clarification and decide whether it meets needs.
Receive criterion-linked feedback: relevance, evidence, comprehensibility, clarification and questions asked.
Try an unseen question/new job advertisement to test transfer; save one concrete next practice goal.
lessons.examplePlan: Outcome email, offer terms, feedback and optional changed-role transfer test.
lessons.action: Read one of three outcomes—offer, rejection or request for clarification—and respond appropriately without assuming a guaranteed next step.
lessons.artifact: A realistic decision and professional reply.
lessons.outcome: Complete the entire fictional journey and identify an independent next action.

lessons.title: Close the loop and transfer to real life
lessons.question: What do you do with the experience after the simulation?
beats: Review what actually happened and what remains uncertain.
Save reusable evidence, personal phrases, and messages while avoiding retention of sensitive personal information.
Choose the next independent action: revise materials, follow up appropriately, seek more openings or prepare for another interview.
lessons.examplePlan: A personal timeline and artifacts collected during the fictional Northstar application.
lessons.action: Identify two communication strengths, one specific weakness, and one next application task; do a different-role transfer check.
lessons.artifact: A portable one-page job-search communication plan.
lessons.outcome: Learner can state a concrete next action without relying on a scripted template.
